Environmental Ed Day 5 Fostering Creativity

Sep 23, 2010 • Janice Cotcher

This morning we chatted on Skype with an outdoor educator who is going to run across Canada to promote getting youth outside and active. The main point he tried to get across: it doesn’t matter what you do, get your kids outside! How sedentary our lifestyles have become. The current generation of elementary and high school students will be the first not to live longer than their parents. Kids spend more time in front of a screen (TV, computer) than sleeping on a daily basis.

This wasn’t really discussed in class but made me think about how kids today do not know how to play. Okay, I realize that is a huge generalization but many don’t. How many kids know how to entertain themselves? Growing up, my family used to take long road trips once a summer. Sometimes we would listen to audio tapes but most of the time my dad found music to be too distracting for his driving. I don’t ever remember being bored: we’d tell stories, we’d play games, we’d fight, we’d sleep but and even once I even recited the about first 45 minutes of Anne of Green Gables. Now for many families, car trips aren’t even a break from the TV.

I have a theory about why kids don’t know how to play: adults are stifling creativity. Parents LET their children sit in front of the TV and computer for hours on end. What ever happened to “Go outside and be back by supper”? Some parents fill up their kids time with so many activities that they don’t have time to play. A lot of creativity comes from being forced outside to find our own entertainment.

Similarly the education system is stifling creativity. I came across this video today:

The video actually reminded me of the book The Little Prince:

Once when I was six years old I saw a magnificent picture in a book, called True Stories from Nature, about the primeval forest. It was a picture of a boa constrictor in the act of swallowing an animal. Here is a copy of the drawing. [!]Drawing of a boa constrictor In the book it said: “Boa constrictors swallow their prey whole, without chewing it. After that they are not able to move, and they sleep through the six months that they need for digestion.”

I pondered deeply, then, over the adventures of the jungle. And after some work with a colored pencil I succeeded in making my first drawing. My Drawing Number One. It looked like this: [!]Coloured drawing of a boa constrictor

I showed my masterpiece to the grown-ups, and asked them whether the drawing frightened them.

But they answered: “Frighten? Why should any one be frightened by a hat?”

My drawing was not a picture of a hat. It was a picture of a boa constrictor digesting an elephant. But since the grown-ups were not able to understand it, I made another drawing: I drew the inside of the boa constrictor, so that the grown-ups could see it clearly. They always need to have things explained. My Drawing Number Two looked like this: [!]Drawing of a boa constrictor with an elephant inside The grown-ups’ response, this time, was to advise me to lay aside my drawings of boa constrictors, whether from the inside or the outside, and devote myself instead to geography, history, arithmetic and grammar. That is why, at the age of six, I gave up what might have been a magnificent career as a painter. I had been disheartened by the failure of my Drawing Number One and my Drawing Number Two. Grown-ups never understand anything by themselves, and it is tiresome for children to be always and forever explaining things to them.

So then I chose another profession, and learned to pilot airplanes. I have flown a little over all parts of the world; and it is true that geography has been very useful to me. At a glance I can distinguish China from Arizona. If one gets lost in the night, such knowledge is valuable.

In the course of this life I have had a great many encounters with a great many people who have been concerned with matters of consequence. I have lived a great deal among grown-ups. I have seen them intimately, close at hand. And that hasn’t much improved my opinion of them.

Whenever I met one of them who seemed to me at all clear-sighted, I tried the experiment of showing him my Drawing Number One, which I have always kept. I would try to find out, so, if this was a person of true understanding. But, whoever it was, he, or she, would always say:

“That is a hat.”

Then I would never talk to that person about boa constrictors, or primeval forests, or stars. I would bring myself down to his level. I would talk to him about bridge, and golf, and politics, and neckties. And the grown-up would be greatly pleased to have met such a sensible man.

  • The Little Prince, Chapter 1 - Antoine de Saint Exupéry

At this point, you may be wondering: What does the Little Prince have to do with Physics education? Actually quite a bit. Although not given also credit, science is a creative pursuit. Problem solving, theories, discovery and innovation are all common in science but how could they be possible without a creative mind? Creativity needs to fostered in all aspects of the students life because our future just may depend on it.
